mechanism: %tx-request-best-candidate (src/networking/protocol.lisp:513-528) selects preferred (outbound) peers first and then the EARLIEST ready time, with the strict comparison (< ready (cdr best)) so exact ties keep whichever entry the list holds first. It is used by both the scheduler (:530) and the expiry failover (:586). Core computes a Priority per announcement as CSipHasher(m_k0, m_k1).Write(txhash).Write(peer).Finalize() >> 1, with the preferred bit in bit 63 (refs/bitcoin/src/txrequest.cpp:103-124), where m_k0/m_k1 are per-node random salts, and selects the highest -- i.e. restrict to preferred peers if any exist, then pick uniformly at random among the candidates, with the choice differing per transaction and unpredictable to an attacker (refs/bitcoin/src/txrequest.h:66-72). The divergence is acknowledged in our own file comment at src/networking/protocol.lisp:321-325; that does not make it absent.
consequence: Announcement order is entirely under the announcer's control, so a peer that races the network's announcements takes the request deterministically instead of with probability 1/(number of preferred candidates), and takes it for EVERY transaction rather than a random subset. Executed: our winner is a function of announcement order and has no dependence on the txhash at all, and an attacker holding A preferred connections that announce first holds exactly A consecutive GETDATA_TX_INTERVAL windows -- 1, 3 and 5 windows for A = 1, 3 and 5, identical in all 20 trials each -- which is the worst case of Core's distribution, obtained every time and chosen by the attacker. Core's txrequest.h:78-84 models the delay as k * GETDATA_TX_INTERVAL with k a hypergeometric random variable precisely because the pick is random; we make k its maximum, deterministically. S2: a concrete censorship lever with an attacker-controlled trigger; not S1, since the transaction still arrives after the attacker's windows expire, and not S3, since the divergence is the difference between a random and a chosen worst case rather than a bounded numeric drift.
evidence: The finder marked this read-both-trees; it is now executed. (1) ga11-p4-selection-is-order-not-hash, 5 equally-preferred announcers over 200 distinct txhashes: (:SAME-ORDER-WINNER-DISTRIBUTION (0 0 0 0 200) :ROTATED-ORDER-WINNER-DISTRIBUTION (40 40 40 40 40)) -- with a fixed announcement order one peer wins all 200, and rotating the order moves the wins with it exactly, so the choice depends on order only and never on the hash. The rotated line is the positive control: a hash-salted selection would have produced a spread independent of the rotation. (2) ga11-p4-earliest-ready-wins, distinct ready times, 100 distinct hashes: (:TRIALS 100 :EARLIEST-ANNOUNCER-WINS 100). (3) ga11-p4-deterministic-across-trackers: the winner index takes only the first or the last announced position across 20 trials (never anything else and never hash-dependent), the two cases being distinct-tick and same-tick announcement times. (4) ga11-p4-consecutive-windows-2 with spaced announcements and backdated expiry: (:ATTACKER-CONNS 3 :HONEST-CONNS 5 :CONSECUTIVE-ATTACKER-WINDOWS (3) :TRIALS 20), and likewise (1) for A=1/H=8 and (5) for A=5/H=3 -- a single value in every case, i.e. zero variance. fix_shape: Port Core's PriorityComputer. Draw two 64-bit salts once at node start (Core's FastRandomContext pair, kept for the life of the process so the ordering is stable per transaction but unpredictable across nodes), and give %tx-request-best-candidate a priority function siphash(k0, k1, txhash || peer-id) >> 1 with the preferred bit ORed into bit 63, selecting the MAXIMUM priority among ready, selectable candidates instead of the earliest ready time; the preferred-first behaviour then falls out of the top bit exactly as it does in Core, and the expiry failover at retry-timed-out-tx-requests uses the same function so the two selection sites cannot diverge. Announcement time keeps its existing role -- gating readiness through the NONPREF / TXID_RELAY / OVERLOADED delays -- and stops deciding the winner. bl.crypto already has SipHash for the addrman and reconciliation short-ids, so the priority is a few lines; the test that pins it is the rotated-order probe above, which must stop tracking the announcement order once the salt is in place, plus a determinism check that a fixed salt reproduces a fixed winner.
